title: Ranabaali: A Sincere Famine Epic That Wins Respect but Tests Patience
excerpt: Reviewers honour the famine subject and the craft — and nearly all of them ask why a film this sincere needed to be this slow.
body:
• Critics rate Ranabaali between 2 and 3.5 out of 5 — sincerity and craft praised, pacing faulted almost everywhere
  • The famine subject is a first for Telugu cinema, and the cinematography and production design draw the strongest notices
  • Vijay Deverakonda's earnest turn and Rashmika Mandanna's Jayamma are the emotional core reviewers point to
  • A predictable second half, a weak background score and an overlong runtime are the recurring complaints
https://youtube.com/watch?v=A36nagDzugo

Telugu cinema has told the British-raj rebellion story many times, but rarely this one: the Great Famine of the 1870s, when grain was shipped out of a starving Madras Presidency to London while Rayalaseema buried its dead. Rahul Sankrityan's Ranabaali plants its hero — Singanamala Bobbili Ranabaali, played by Vijay Deverakonda — in that famine, against a British commissioner, Sir Theodore Hector (Arnold Vosloo), who promises record grain exports and imposes heavy taxes and forced railway labour on villages that have nothing left. It is the first screen pairing of Vijay Deverakonda and Rashmika Mandanna since their real-life wedding, and the costliest film of his career. Critics have responded with respect for the attempt and frustration at the execution — a split that runs through nearly every review.

The consensus

Published ratings spread from 2 to 3.5 out of 5, and the reviews read like variations on one sentence: sincere film, slow telling. Cinema Express, at 2.5, calls it a sincere attempt that loses its way; 123telugu, at 2.75, finds sincere effort but only moderate impact; IndustryHit, warmer at 3.25, praises an honest, conviction-driven period drama that refuses to sugar-coat the famine. The praise is consistent about the film's craft and its two leads; the criticism is just as consistent about pacing, a predictable second half and a runtime that needed trimming. Nobody calls it a cynical film. Several call it a tiring one.

What's praised

The craft, first. IndustryHit singles out the cinematography of Jishnu Bhattacharjee and Nirav Shah as one of the film's biggest assets, capturing the dry lands, forts and villages of nineteenth-century Rayalaseema with stunning authenticity, and gives the production design a special mention — barring a few hill portions, it never feels like a set. The famine itself is shown plainly, and reviewers credit Sankrityan's conviction in refusing to soften a chapter of history that, as 123telugu notes, Telugu cinema has not explored before.

The performances carry the emotional case. 123telugu calls Vijay Deverakonda earnest as the rebel leader, strong in the action sequences, and finds Rashmika Mandanna impressive as Jayamma, whose attempts to change her stone-hearted husband give the film its sweet spot — their romance is the relief and the highlight in a grave drama. FilmyCycle, the most generous notice at 3.5, calls it Vijay's one-man show, praising his makeover and his Rayalaseema slang. Ajay-Atul's melodies also register: the song between Vijay and Rashmika is singled out by IndustryHit, even from reviewers cooler on the film overall.

What's criticized

The second half, again — but here the complaint is weight, not noise. 123telugu says the film picks up momentum with the Jayamma chapter and a decent interval block, then gets bogged down in a predictable, below-par second half, with the lengthy runtime a major shortcoming. Cinema Express argues the ambition to surface a hidden chapter of Anantapur's history outruns the storytelling. The toughest notices go further: Venky Reviews calls the screenplay dead slow and the background score a huge letdown, arguing the film lacks the emotional connect a subject like this needs. Even IndustryHit, praising the film, concedes the BGM could have been stronger and that the editing, impressive in the first half, needed more trimming in the second. When a film's admirers and detractors file the same two complaints — pace and score — they are usually the true ones.

What this means for you

For diaspora audiences, Ranabaali is a considered weekend choice rather than a mass entertainer: a serious Telugu period drama about a famine many families' histories touch, carried by the Vijay–Rashmika pairing in their first film as a married couple — itself a draw across the US Telugu circuit. Go in expecting a slow burn and a long sit; viewers who value the subject and the craft will find plenty to respect, and viewers looking for the pace of a typical Vijay Deverakonda entertainer should wait for streaming.

data_cards.rating_consensus: Critics respect Ranabaali more than they enjoy it: an honest, beautifully mounted famine drama with committed leads, weighed down by a slow, predictable second half — a film to admire, at a pace you have to accept.
